              1  Introduction

                 World models (WM)  [1, 2, 3] have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied decision-
                making [4, 5, 6, 7]. By learning predictive models of environment dynamics, they enable test-
                   time reasoning and the synthesis of novel behaviors for unseen goals by searching in the action
                   space [8, 9, 10, 11]. However, planning with WMs faces two fundamental challenges: 1) searcharXiv:2610.42146v1
                  complexity grows exponentially with planning horizon, and 2) prediction errors accumulate over
                   long rollouts. Therefore, most WM-based planners are restricted to short-horizon tasks [8, 9], rely
                 on simplified action abstractions [10], or operate in high-level spaces such as language, sacrificing
                     fine-grained control [12].

                    Hierarchical learning offers a principled solution to this scalability challenge by decomposing long-
                   horizon problems into manageable abstractions [13, 14, 15].  It has been extensively studied in
                  Reinforcement Learning (RL) [16, 17, 18, 19], where hierarchy mitigates the credit assignment
                  problem in long trajectories, and in imitation learning [20, 21], where it enables reusable behaviors.
               More recently, hierarchical structure has been introduced into diffusion-based planners to avoid
                      directly modeling entire trajectories [22, 23, 24], improving scalability and generalization beyond
                    fixed-horizon training data.

             How can we enable the same capabilities for task-agnostic world models, enabling long-horizon zero-
                     shot planning for unseen goals? A direct approach would be to simply increase the prediction horizon

or action abstraction (e.g., frame-skipping) [25]. However, previous attempts at hierarchical world
models typically depend on task-specific priors to function effectively, relying on pre-trained skills
and low-level policies [19, 26] or rewards and value functions to verify subgoal feasibility [27, 28].
This dependency arises because planning is fundamentally adversarial: without these anchoring
constraints, a powerful optimizer will inevitably exploit deficiencies in a learned world model,
discovering "wormholes" or unrealistic transitions [29, 30]. To make hierarchical world models
suitable for planning, we must construct a latent space that both condenses trajectory information
to minimize search complexity, and remains inherently well-behaved to prevent the planner from
exploiting unrealistic transitions.

To this end, we introduce ID-WM, a hierarchical world model with implicit dynamics grounded
in the insight that effective planning requires decoupling topological reachability from execution
details (Figure 1). ID-WM consists of a high-level diffusion-based world model that only implicitly
models the dynamics by outputting states that are within a fixed distance away from the current state,
functioning as a neighboring state generator, and a deterministic low-level model conditioned on both
current state and action, acting as an inverse dynamics solver. Conditioned on the current state and a
Gaussian noise, the high-level model leverages the generative power of diffusion to map a tractable
unit Gaussian latent space to the manifold of feasible neighboring states. This formulation allows us
to treat the noise as an implicit high-level action, enabling the planner to search over a well-behaved
distribution instead of complex, discontinuous skill spaces to reason purely about "where to go,"
while the low-level model recovers the precise executable actions for "how to get there."

We summarize our contributions as follows:

        • We introduce ID-WM, a hierarchical world model that decouples reachability from control,
         eliminating the need for task-specific value functions or pre-trained policies.
        • We propose a corresponding hierarchical planning algorithm that bridges high-level abstrac-
         tion with local dynamics, enabling robust, long-horizon decision-making.
        • Across three navigation and manipulation environment suites, ID-WM shows 38.5% im-
        provement for reaching arbitrary goals against powerful hierarchical offline reinforcement
         learning, imitation learning, and diffusion planning methods, and crucially, a 135% improve-
       ment over single-level world model and planning regimes.


2  Related Work

2.1  Hierarchical Learning

Hierarchical learning has long been a foundational pursuit in artificial intelligence, decomposing
long-horizon problems into manageable abstractions [13, 14, 15].  This paradigm spans policy


                                       2

architectures [31], reinforcement learning [16, 18, 27, 32], imitation learning [20], and planning [28,
33]. Existing work focuses on both behavioral (skills/options) [14, 19, 26, 34, 35, 36, 37] and
subgoal-centric approaches [17, 28, 38]. However, these methods typically rely on coupled priors,
such as rewards, learned value functions or pre-trained low-level policies [28, 32] to ensure feasibility,
limiting generalization beyond the training distribution. In contrast, we eliminate this dependency,
enabling robust hierarchical reasoning purely through implicit dynamics even when reliable value
functions and policies are absent.

2.2  World Models for Embodied Planning

World models [1, 2, 3] have emerged as a foundational paradigm for embodied decision-making,
enabling agents to reason about the future consequences of their actions. Recently, the field has shifted
towards developing general-purpose world models [5, 8, 10, 39, 40, 41] capable of capturing broad
environmental dynamics, diverging from traditional model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL)
where learning task-specific reward or value functions is paramount [42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48].
Once these dynamics are learned, inference-time planning algorithms like the Cross-Entropy Method
(CEM) [49] or gradient descent—are employed to derive behaviors zero-shot [8, 9, 11, 50]. However,
the effectiveness of these approaches is often constrained to short horizons due to the computational
complexity of search and the accumulation of prediction errors over time. While various strategies
have been proposed to mitigate these issues, ranging from robust gradient-based optimization [30, 51]
and efficient sampling routines [52] to temporal approximations for longer action sequences [10],
they remain fundamentally flat in their temporal reasoning. Consequently, they struggle with long-
horizon task solving, remaining susceptible to local minima and limited in their scalability to complex
behaviors. Concurrently, HWM [25] builds a hierarchical latent world model by increasing the
high-level frameskip and learning macro-actions; in contrast, ID-WM searches over the diffusion
noise space, which is smooth and well-conditioned by construction.

2.3  Diffusion Models and Planning

Diffusion probabilistic models [53, 54, 55] excel at capturing complex, multimodal distributions
via iterative denoising.  Their efficacy is proven across high-dimensional modalities, including
pixels [40, 41, 56, 57], language [58], and robot actions [59, 60]. Recently, diffusion models have
been proposed as zero-shot planners for embodied tasks [61, 62, 63, 64]. These methods model entire
trajectories directly, limiting generalization to out-of-distribution initial-goal pairs and constraining
planning horizons to those seen during training. While hierarchical formulations mitigate these
constraints, they rely on task-specific value functions [22, 23, 32], successful task trajectories [65], or
assumed access to low-level primitives [24]. In contrast, we redefine diffusion as a local generator
rather than a global planner. By delegating long-horizon reasoning to search, our method composes
local jumps into novel trajectories without requiring task-specific priors.

3  Hierarchical World Models with Implicit Dynamics

Overview and Problem Formulation. We consider a goal-conditioned planning problem within a
Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined by the tuple M = (S, A, P), where S is the continuous
state space, A is the action space, and P(st+1|s≤t, a≤t) represents the transition dynamics.

Following prior world modeling methods [8, 10, 11], we learn environment dynamics from a task-
agnostic offline dataset without any reward labeling via a world model, and plan to reach arbitrary
unseen goals at test time. More specifically, an agent is provided with an initial state o0 and a goal
state og at test time. The objective is to execute a sequence of actions (a0, a1, . . . , aT −1) such that
the distance between the agent’s final state oT and the goal og is minimized. Unlike prior work, we do
not assume a fixed task horizon T [8], focusing instead on enabling the agent to perform autonomous
long-horizon reasoning and planning.

3.1  Hierarchical World Models with Implicit Dynamics

model and a low-level inverse dynamics model. As illustrated in Figure 2, the high-level model
operates as a reachable state generator, predicting a distribution of feasible future states conditioned

3.1.1  High-level Implicit Dynamics Model

To model the manifold of reachable states without restricting the agent to a fixed set of discrete skills,
we formulate the high-level world model as a conditional diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) [54].
Let x0 represent the target future state st+∆(at a fixed temporal offset ∆). The forward diffusion
process q(xj|xj−1) gradually adds Gaussian noise to the data according to a variance schedule
β1, . . . , βK:

Implicit High-Level Action Space. A key insight of our approach is to treat the initial noise vector
zt as an implicit high-level action. Unlike discrete skill indices or learned latent codes which may
suffer from mode collapse or topological discontinuities, illustrated in Section 6.13, the noise space
Z = Rd is inherently smooth and well-behaved (isotropic Gaussian). By optimizing over zt, the
planner searches over the standard Gaussian latent space, where any sample z maps to a physically
valid reachable state on the data manifold via the deterministic DDIM mapping.

3.1.2  Low-level World Model

The high-level World Model (WM) provides long-horizon guidance by identifying target states, yet
it lacks the granular transition dynamics necessary to prescribe executable actions. To this end, we
employ a transformer-based deterministic low-level WM following Zhou et al. [8], which functions
as an inverse dynamics model through planning.

Given a history of states st−k:t and actions at−k:t, the low-level WM predicts the next state ˆst+1 =
flo(st−k:t, at−k:t). The model is trained via supervised learning to minimize the prediction error:

                       L = ∥ˆst+1 −st+1∥2                                      (4)

Consistent with Zhou et al. [8], we utilize an MLP action encoder to process raw action sequences
before they are input into the transformer backbone.

At inference, we leverage this model for inverse dynamics through planning. Given a target state
s∗, we search for an optimal action sequence (a0, . . . , aHlo−1) over a low-level planning horizon
Hlo such that the planning cost ∥ˆsHlo −s∗∥2 is minimized. We detail the full hierarchical planning
procedure in Section 3.2.

3.2  Hierarchical Planning with ID-WM

At inference, given an initial state o0 and a goal state og, we employ hierarchical planning to
determine a sequence of actions that reaches og. We formulate this as a Model Predictive Control
(MPC) problem, where each iteration consists of two phases: subgoal generation and subgoal
realization. The overall hierarchical planning procedure is detailed in Algorithm 1. We also include
a full version in Algorithm 2. Throughout, ∆denotes the temporal radius of each subgoal (the
maximum number of environment steps between consecutive subgoals), Hhi the number of subgoals
per high-level plan, and Hlo the low-level planning horizon used to reach each subgoal.

Subgoal Search via High-level WM. In the first phase, we identify a sequence of latent subgoals
s∗0, . . . , s∗Hhi such that s∗0 = s0 and s∗Hhi = sg. To ensure that each subgoal remains within the
reachable manifold of the low-level WM given its search budget, we constrain the distance between
consecutive subgoals s∗i , s∗i+1 to be no more than ∆environment steps. We optimize the latent noise
variables z0, . . . , zHhi−1 using the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) to minimize the following planning
cost:
                    L = ∥ˆsHhi −sg∥2 + αLreg(Z)                                (5)
where Lreg is a regularization term designed to keep the sampled noise within the support of the
standard Gaussian distribution. This prevents the planner from exploiting adversarial regions of the
latent space that would result in out-of-distribution transitions during DDIM sampling.

Subgoal Realization via Low-level WM. We similarly employ the CEM optimizer to identify
the executable action sequences required to reach each intermediate subgoal. The agent plans and

executes actions to reach the immediate subgoal, proceeding sequentially through the high-level
trajectory. Upon completing the sequence for all subgoals generated by the high-level WM, the agent
initiates a new MPC iteration to replan the high-level trajectory from its current state.

Latent Noise Regularization. While the latent space is theoretically structured as a unit Gaussian,
unconstrained planning can favor adversarial latents that produce unrealistic state transitions. To

4  Experiments

Our experiments are designed to answer the following key questions:

        • Subgoal Generation: Can ID-WM reliably generate diverse and feasible reachable states?

        • Generalization: Can ID-WM solve long-horizon planning tasks to reach arbitrary, zero-
         shot goals at test time?

        • Scaling: How does the performance of ID-WM scale across environments of increasing
        complexity?

        • Visual Planning:  Is ID-WM effective for long-horizon planning directly from high-
        dimensional visual observations?

4.2  Baselines

We compare ID-WM with five state-of-the-art offline learning methods including imitation learning
(GCBC), offline RL (HIQL), diffusion planners (Diffuser, Hierarchical Diffuser), and planning with
world models (Single-level WM with MPC). See Section 6.4 for full details.

4.3  Generating Neighboring States with ID-WM

We first investigate the extent to which each level of ID-WM accurately captures the underlying
data distribution and predicts future states across varying temporal granularities. Specifically, for
the high-level WM, we evaluate whether sampling from the latent prior yields diverse and reachable
future states.

In Figure 4, we sample 100 latent noise vectors z ∼N(0, I) and visualize the resulting generated
states ˆs∆= fhi(s0, z, ∆) reachable within a ∆-step horizon. For each ∆, we overlay all 100
generated samples to visualize the predicted state distribution, explicitly marking the agent’s position
with a black dot for clarity.

As illustrated in Figure 4, the high-level WM generates diverse and physically reachable states for
both the Wall and PushT environments. In the Wall environment, the dispersion of agent positions
increases with ∆, reflecting a larger reachable radius as the temporal budget grows. Similarly, in
the PushT environment, we observe an increasingly diffused distribution of both the agent and the
T-block. The smooth coverage of object configurations demonstrates that the model successfully
captures the complex, multi-modal interactions between the agent and the object. This high-fidelity
distribution modeling serves as a necessary prerequisite for planning, enabling the system to generate
diverse trajectories and generalize effectively to unseen goals in downstream tasks.

4.4  Hierarchical Planning with ID-WM

Can ID-WM solve long-horizon planning tasks to reach arbitrary, zero-shot goals at test time? To
this end, we conduct hierarchical planning on three environment suites.

For all environments and baselines, we randomly sample 50 pairs of initial and goal states, with
sampling method detailed in Section 6.2, and report the average performance across these instances.
For the PushT task, we report two metrics: the success rate and the final coverage of the T-block
relative to the target configuration. A trial is considered successful only if both the agent and the
T-block reach their respective goal positions. In contrast, the final coverage metric provides a more
granular measure of performance by focusing specifically on the object’s alignment. To further
evaluate generalization capabilities, we test PushT under two settings: a standard regime and a
data-augmented regime featuring random spatial transformations and rotations. All experiments are
conducted with a maximum horizon of 2000 environment steps. For all experiments, ID-WM uses
∆= 5 (25 environment steps with frameskip) and Hhi = 5 subgoals per high-level plan, without
per-task tuning; the planner replans after each executed plan (up to 15 replans), so no prior knowledge
of the goal distance is required. We ablate ∆and the number of subgoals in Section 6.7.

In Table 1, ID-WM outperforms all baselines, achieving a 38.5% overall improvement and 135%
gain over single-level WM with MPC (SL-WM). The gap is most evident in PushT with random

While SL-WM performs well on shorter horizons (Maze, Wall), it fails on PushT’s long-horizon

4.5  How does ID-WM scale with task complexity?

We investigate whether ID-WM scales to tasks of increasing complexity across two dimensions:
environment size and goal horizon.

Scaling with Maze Size. We evaluate ID-WM across four mazes of increasing difficulty: U-Maze
(3 × 3), Medium Maze (6 × 6), Large Maze (7 × 10), and Giant Maze (13 × 13) (Figure 7a). Each
dataset contains 2,000 random 100-step trajectories. Given a fixed dataset size, data coverage naturally
becomes sparser as maze size increases.

While all methods achieve near-perfect success on the U-Maze, baselines degrade significantly in
larger environments (Figure 7a). In contrast, ID-WM maintains the highest performance on the
Large Maze. We hypothesize this is because ID-WM combines local dynamics modeling with
high-level planning, effectively "stitching" together regions of sparse data. Unlike GCBC or Diffuser
(which model entire trajectories simultaneously) or HIQL (which requires dense data for global value
functions), ID-WM does not rely on global trajectory coverage. Furthermore, while H-Diffuser
uses abstraction, it lacks an explicit dynamics model, resulting in brittle plans requiring expensive,


                                       9

high-frequency replanning. By grounding its hierarchy in explicit local dynamics, ID-WM generates
robust, scalable plans.

Scaling with Goal Horizon. Building on the PushT planning benchmark introduced by Zhou et al.
[8] (which evaluates goals 25 steps away), we increase complexity by sampling goals from the
validation set that are d ∈{25, 50, . . . , 150} steps away.

We compare ID-WM against a single-level world model baseline that performs full-horizon CEM
search and replanning at every step. While the total number of executed actions is identical, ID-WM
achieves a near-perfect success rate across all horizons as shown in Figure 7b). This confirms our main
PushT results (Table 1), demonstrating that ID-WM maintains precise goal-reaching capabilities
even when goals are over 150 steps away.


4.6  Vision-based Planning with ID-WM

To evaluate ID-WM in high-dimensional observation spaces, we test it on a vision-based PushT
task. We use the state-based PushT dataset augmented with four 90◦rotations for spatial robustness.
Observations (3 × 64 × 64 images) are encoded into 4 × 8 × 8 latents using a pretrained Stable
Diffusion VAE [66]. We compare against AVDC [64], a language-conditioned video planner that

5  Conclusion

We present ID-WM, a hierarchical world modeling and planning framework that decouples tem-
porally extended subgoal generation from local reachability. By treating diffusion noise as implicit
actions, we constrain the planning search space to a unit Gaussian, ensuring reliable subgoal gener-
ation. ID-WM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and demonstrates high-quality
vision-based subgoal generation. Ultimately, grounding hierarchical abstraction in explicit local
dynamics represents a promising step toward robust, long-horizon decision-making.

Limitations. First, ID-WM’s reliance on search-based optimization within a diffusion latent space
incurs higher inference times than reactive policies or deterministic world models. Future work will
explore amortized or gradient-based planning to mitigate this bottleneck. Second, while our hierarchy
prevents planning complexity from scaling with trajectory length, it still scales with state-space
dimensionality. Integrating compact, structured representation learning could further streamline this
planning process for highly complex environments.

6  Appendix

6.1  Environments and Dataset Generation

We evaluate ID-WM on three navigation and manipulation environment suites as shown in Figure 3.
The environments are Wall, PushT, and Maze, with task horizon ranging from hundreds to thousands
of environment steps.

 a) Wall: Introduced in Zhou et al. [8], this is a simple 2D navigation environment that consists of
    two rooms separated by a wall with a door. The agent’s goal is to navigate from a random starting
    location on one side of the wall to a random location on the other side, requiring the agent to
    pass through the door. We use the same dataset as in Zhou et al. [8], which consists of randomly
    generated 1920 trajectories of length 50.
 b) Maze:  This environment is introduced in Fu et al. [67], where a force-actuated 2-DoF ball
    navigates to an arbitrary location in a maze. In this work, we consider maze layout of four sizes,
  U (3 × 3), Medium (6 × 6), Large (7 × 10), and Giant (13 × 13), visualized in Figure 7 a). We
    generate 2000 random trajectories of length 100 for each maze layout.
 c) PushT: Introduced by Chi et al. [59], this environment consists of a pusher agent and a T-shaped
    block. The objective is for both the agent and the block to reach specified target locations from
   random initial positions. We evaluate two variants of this task: in Fix Goal, the target state is
    a fixed configuration (the green T); in Random Goal, the target is randomly sampled from the
    environment’s state space. Both settings are significantly more challenging than the formulation
    in Zhou et al. [8], where the goal is provided at a known, fixed horizon of 25 steps. In contrast,
    completing the task in our settings often requires hundreds of steps, rendering standard single-
    level planning infeasible. Following [8], we train on noisy, replayed trajectories. We further
    evaluate our method in a data-abundant regime by applying random translation and rotation
    augmentations to the existing dataset.

6.2  Task Visualizations

For the Wall, PushT, Giant Maze, Large Maze, Medium Maze, and U-Maze environments, we
randomly sample 50 initial and goal states from each environment’s state space (visualizations in
Figure 9). For PushT, the random-goal setting samples both the initial and goal states randomly
from the environment, whereas the fixed-goal setting samples a random initial state while using the
environment’s fixed goal location. For the Wall environment, to ensure sufficient task difficulty, the
initial and final object locations are constrained to lie on opposite sides of the wall. For the Giant
Maze, Large Maze, Medium Maze, and U-Maze environments, we follow the random state sampling
procedure used in OGBench: we sample arbitrary free cells for the ball and add continuous uniform
noise around the corresponding grid-cell centers.

6.3  Data Augmentation

Data augmentation for PushT.  For PushT we additionally apply geometric data augmentation to
the offline dataset at each training step. The state vector contains end-effector position and velocity
(xdot, ydot, ˙xdot, ˙ydot), T-block position (xT , yT ), and T-block orientation (sin θT , cos θT ). One of
three augmentation types is sampled per step:

        • Displacement (40%): all positions shifted by a random integer offset (δx, δy) chosen so
          that both the end-effector and the T-block remain within the screen boundaries [50, 450] and
         [100, 400] respectively.
        • Rotation (30%): all positions and the T-block angle rotated by θ ∼U(0, 2π) about the
        scene center; velocities and actions are rotated accordingly.
        • Displacement + Rotation (30%): a half-range displacement combined with a small rotation
        θ ∼U(0, 30◦).

6.11.5  HIQL [18]

HIQL decomposes offline goal-conditioned RL into two levels of hierarchy. A high-level policy
proposes a subgoal representation ϕ([s; w]), where w is an intermediate waypoint state sampled from
the same trajectory, and a low-level policy executes primitive actions to reach that subgoal. Both
policies are trained offline via Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) using a shared implicit value
function Vθ(s, g).

The value function is trained with an IQL-style expectile regression objective:

         LV (θV ) = E(s,s′)∼D, g∼p(g|τ) Lτ2  r(s, g) + γV¯θV (s′, g) −VθV (s, g)    .

where Lτ2 denotes the asymmetric squared expectile loss with parameter τ. Given the shared value
function, both policies are updated via AWR. For the low-level policy πl, the advantage measures
progress toward subgoal w. For the high-level policy πh, the advantage measures progress toward
the final goal g upon reaching subgoal w.

6.11.6  Diffuser [61]

Diffuser frames offline goal-conditioned planning as a trajectory denoising problem. A temporal
U-Net processes a full trajectory τ = (s0, a0, . . . , sH−1, aH−1) of planning horizon H, and iterative

specified goal state. At inference, the current state is inpainted at the start of the trajectory and the
goal state at the end; the remaining timesteps are filled by denoising. All environments share the
same base configuration. Only the planning horizon H is adjusted (in Table 16).

covers a larger temporal horizon at lower computational cost. A low-level diffusion model then plans
a dense trajectory of length Hll between consecutive subgoals, conditioned on the current state and

We further analyze the training-time convergence behavior of the high-level world model, extending
the qualitative study in Figure 4. While Figure 4 visualizes the final learned neighboring-state

Specifically, we fix validation observations s0 and periodically sample predicted future states from

z ∼N(0, I). Each column corresponds to a different number of training steps on a logarithmic scale:

As training begins, the predicted distributions are highly dispersed and often fail to preserve the
structure of the PushT scene. In early checkpoints, the sampled futures do not consistently respect
the local geometry of the object or the physically plausible displacement induced by the agent-object
interaction. As training progresses, the generated samples become increasingly concentrated around
coherent future configurations. By approximately 200 to 600 training steps, the model begins to
capture the coarse reachable region for each temporal horizon, and later checkpoints further sharpen
the predicted distribution while preserving meaningful sample diversity.
